prompt.context: Our client is a start-up with the ability to deliver broadband internet to commercial airlines. The start-up would have to invest relatively little up front and would keep most of the revenues. They would charge customers on a per-flight pricing model.
prompt.question: How would you help them think about their offering? Specifically, should the client enter this market?

clarifying_info.q: How many planes are in scope?
What does the client need to earn per plane to be profitable?
clarifying_info.a: If the company can generate $250,000 per plane in annual revenue, they will be profitable installing the technology on that plane.

clarifying_info.q: How many legs does each plane fly per year?

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1
exhibits.shows: A table with data to help estimate market size, showing seat counts, load factors, and business traveler mix by cabin class (First and Coach).
exhibits.data: First class: 20 seats/plane, 0.75 load factor; Coach: 180 seats/plane, 0.75 load factor; Business travelers: 100% in First, 30% in Coach

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2
exhibits.shows: A pricing/penetration table showing number of users out of 100 passengers at various price points per flight.

framework: Industry & Market attractiveness: size, growth, key players
Market sizing: estimate number of potential users (laptop-carrying business travelers) per flight
Pricing analysis: determine revenue-maximizing price point using Exhibit 2
Profitability / breakeven: check if per-plane revenue at chosen price exceeds the $250,000 breakeven threshold
Competitive landscape: IP/patent protection, low-speed alternatives
Recommendation: synthesize into a clear go/no-go with supporting reasons

questions.prompt: Estimate the total annual potential user-legs (market size).
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through a structured bottoms-up calculation using Exhibit 1: fill seats by load factor, apply business-traveler mix to get laptop users per plane, multiply by fleet size and legs per year.

math.setup: First class filled seats: 20 x 0.75 = 15; Coach filled seats: 180 x 0.75 = 135. Laptop users: First = 15 x 100% = 15; Coach = 135 x 30% = 40.5. Total laptop users per plane ≈ 55.5 ≈ 50 (rounded). Annual user-legs = 3,000 planes x 2,000 legs/plane x 50 users/leg.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what price per flight should the client charge?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate revenue per 100 passengers at each price point and identify the maximum. $15 yields the highest revenue at $300 per 100 passengers.

math.setup: Revenue = price x number of users per 100 passengers at that price.

questions.prompt: Conduct a breakeven analysis. At $15/flight, will the client break even on a per-plane basis?
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert the $250,000/plane/year profitability threshold into a required users-per-leg figure, then compare to the estimated 10 users/leg at the 20% penetration rate implied by $15 pricing.

math.setup: Required revenue per leg = $250,000 / 2,000 legs = $125/leg. Required users at $15 = $125 / $15 ≈ 8 users/leg. Estimated actual users = 50 laptop users/leg x 20% penetration = 10 users/leg.
steps: 50 laptop users/leg x 20% penetration = 10 users/leg estimated
math.answer: Yes, the client should break even; estimated 10 users/leg exceeds the required ~8 users/leg.

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors should the client consider before entering this market?

categories.name: Competition & IP
ideas: The company holds the patent on high-speed in-flight broadband, creating a strong barrier to entry
Need to assess low-speed internet alternatives already available on some carriers
Monitor satellite and ground-based connectivity rivals (e.g., Gogo, ViaSat) for potential IP challenges

categories.name: Risks
ideas: Technical reliability at altitude and during weather events
FAA/regulatory approval requirements for onboard hardware
Airline willingness to adopt and install hardware
Passenger adoption slower than projected, especially leisure travelers

categories.name: Revenue model
ideas: Per-flight flat fee vs. time-based or data-capped pricing
Corporate/enterprise subscription plans for frequent business flyers
Tiered speed tiers (basic vs. premium broadband)

categories.name: Go-to-market
ideas: Partner with major carriers first to build installed base
Target routes with highest share of business travelers (e.g., NYC-LAX, transatlantic)
Bundle with airline loyalty programs to drive adoption

recommendation: Enter the market: the breakeven analysis shows the client can be profitable at a $15/flight price point, reaching ~10 users/leg versus the ~8 required
Patent protection on high-speed broadband creates a defensible competitive moat
The total addressable market is large (~300M annual user-legs) and business-traveler demand is strong
risks: Low-speed alternatives could limit willingness to pay at $15
Airline hardware installation timelines and capital constraints could slow roll-out
next_steps: Negotiate pilot installation agreements with 1-2 major airlines
File/reinforce patent portfolio against potential workarounds
Monitor low-speed competitor pricing and refine price point accordingly
Develop corporate subscription offering to raise ARPU
